newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Will the real Al Gore please stand up?
newsitem.headline: Will the real Al Gore please stand up?

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
When Al Gore met a group of South African labour union leaders last weekend, one of them had a request: could the Vice President of the United States please demonstrate his version of the macarena?

Gore's reputation for being stiff and awkward has spread beyond the shores of his homeland. Two days later, he ran into 11-year-old Jacqui Bransky in the lobby of his Cape Town hotel. "Please show us how you do the macarena," she asked, giggling.

Gore first unveiled his mock interpretation of the popular dance, in which he stands completely motionless, at the Democratic Party's National Convention last August. The joke is one of a series he often tells about himself to warm up crowds. Another example: "How do you tell Al Gore in a room full of secret service agents? He's the stiff one."

Gore is in South Africa at the head of a high-level U.S. delegation for three days of talks to deepen cooperation between the two countries on trade, economics, science, education, health and the environment.
His self-deprecating humour has a serious purpose. It is designed to show his lighter, more humorous side and counter the impression that he is a boring, somewhat soulless technocrat.

Now that he is perceived as the leading Democratic contender for the presidency in 2000, Gore needs those jokes more than ever because the truth is, desite all his efforts to loosen up, he is stiff. He still speaks in a formal, slow, jerky manner, with frequent pauses in the middle of his sentences, that tends to put distance between him and his listeners.

Asked by Reuters if he was tired of having to pretend that he is a stand-up comedian, Gore replied: "The premise of your question is that I'm not being myself when I make jokes about stiffness. And I am."

Clearly, on a diplomatic mission overseas, Gore could be expected to make fewer jokes. "Such jokes would have less resonance here because I'm not as familiar and they haven't had enough experience of me to know how stiff I am," he said.

Still, welcoming South African guests to a reception at the U.S. ambassador's residence, he could not resist unleashing one Al Gore joke. "In the United States I'm known as a stiff guy. In Cape Town I'm known as a traffic-blocking guy," he said, referring to media stories blaming Gore's motorcade for traffic jams in Cape Town. "If it happens, talk to the police," he said.

Gore is said to have been studying the techniques of his charismatic boss, President Bill Clinton, whose uncanny skill at bonding with ordinary people is admired even by his most bitter political opponents.

Aides insist Gore is loosening up and wonder when he will start making jokes about the fast-developing bald patch in the middle of his head. They believe it's only a matter of time. For Gore, as for other men, coming to terms with such a painful issue requires some effort, but when one of his political consultants suggested that he take a drug to induce hair growth the vice president brushed the idea aside.

For Gore, foreign diplomatic forays serve an important purpose. They allow him to burnish his leadership credentials while drawing attention away from the constant drip of scandals associated with Democratic political fundraising at home.

Foreign leaders are also beginning to view Gore differently, as Clinton's designated heir-apparent and possibly the next President of the United States. "It makes us pay more attention to him than before. It makes every word more significant," one senior South African official said.

Gore is universally hailed as a world leader of the environmental movement and as such is already beginning to pick up foreign endorsements. In Durban on Friday, South African nationalist Ian Player, brother of the renowned golfer, said: "The vice president is the man who the world knows as the leader on the environment. I pray to God he will be guided to continue to lead the world into the next century."
Gore smiled and said he was unworthy of such praise.
